newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: FOCUS-NZ experts not assured on inflation outlook.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-NZ experts not assured on inflation outlook.

text.p: New Zealand data on Tuesday reinforced the prospect of inflation falling away over the rest of the year, but many analysts remained unconvinced by the central bank's view on prices in the longer term.
March quarter core inflation was a surprisingly weak 0.22 percent, to give an annual rise of 1.97 percent.
The Reserve Bank of New Zealand (RBNZ) had expected 0.5 percent and 2.2 percent, while economists' average forecasts were a fraction below that.

Ahead of the data the debt and currency market had doggedly held monetary conditions tighter than the RBNZ wanted, which many analysts said showed markets were more pessimistic than the bank about prospects of achieving lower inflation.
Conditions loosened on the data, with short debt rates falling sharply and the dollar softening, but still not to the degree the central bank wants, commentators said.
Economists like Stephen Toplis at Doyle Paterson Brown argued that the benign data did not prove the RBNZ right and the market wrong.

"The widely held concern about the bank's perceptions going forward is that as we go into calendar 1998, growth is likely to move above potential. As a consequence of that you're likely to see increased inflationary pressures," he told Reuters. "Certainly from our perspective it (the data) will in no way affect our medium term forecasts."
While the RBNZ sees core inflation as low as 0.8 percent through most of 1998, Doyle Paterson Brown sees it reaching a low of just 1.4 or 1.5 percent before picking up again.
UBS Australia economist Stephen Roberts said the data suggested the fall in inflation this year was likely to be more pronounced than his bank previously thought.
Accordingly, it had revised down its 1997 forecast to 1.3 percent from 1.6 percent.

"However, our 1998 inflation is unchanged at 1.8 percent, implying relatively pronounced pick up in inflation pressures in the coming growth cycle, driven by considerable fiscal pump-priming," Roberts said.
The National-New Zealand First coalition government, formed in December, has said it plans an extra NZ$5 billion spending over the next three years, which is expected to boost inflationary pressures.
WestpacTrust economist Joselyn Stroombergen said Tuesday's data would make the RBNZ more confident it could bring core inflation down to 0.8 percent.

"We've never had any argument with the fact that underlying inflation is probably going to fall quite sharply over the next couple of quarters, and we certainly have it falling under two percent by the end of the year as well, but it's the continuation of that fall in the one to two year time frame that I think there still has to be some doubt about," she said.

However, Bankers Trust New Zealand economist David Plank said that, after fighting the RBNZ for an extended period, markets may now start to believe the bank's inflation outlook where the key aim is to hold core inflation in a range between nought and three percent.
"Today's CPI number is sufficiently 'good' for the market to reconsider its view that the RBNZ's inflation outlook is too optimistic," Plank said.
